0.title: Esther: The Hidden Hand
0.overview:
The book of Esther never names God. In the ESV of its ten chapters the words God, LORD, pray and heaven do not occur once. The Greek translators later added prayers and the name of the Lord, but our Bibles follow the Hebrew. Yet by the last chapter no reader can doubt who has been at work. Esther pictures how God is present in most of his people's lives: not in burning bushes, but in the timing of things.

It is set in Susa under Ahasuerus, whom the Greeks called Xerxes (486-465 BC), a generation before Nehemiah served his son in the same palace, among the Jews who did not go home. The orphan Esther is made queen, keeping her people secret; her cousin Mordecai, a Benjaminite of the family of Kish, will not bow to Haman the Agagite; and Haman, by lot and decree, sets a day for every Jew in the empire to be killed. The old war with Amalek, left unfinished when Saul son of Kish spared Agag (1 Sam 15), is fought again in the Persian court.

Is Esther history? It presents itself as history, citing the royal chronicles (2:23; 10:2), and its picture of Xerxes’ court, palace at Susa, couriers and customs fits what we know of Persia. With the historic confessions, this commentary holds that Scripture as first given is without error, and it reads Esther as a true account. Greek historians name Xerxes’ queen Amestris, but a Persian king had several wives, and the four-year gap between chapters 1 and 2 (1:3; 2:16) fits the years Xerxes was at war in Greece. Persian records are sparse and would not be expected to name a Jewish queen. Why is it in the canon, when God is never named? Some in the early church hesitated over it, but Jews and Christians alike received it as the account of Purim; its silence about God is part of its message: he rules even when unseen.

Then everything turns. Esther, who may have come to the kingdom for such a time as this, goes to the king uncalled: if I perish, I perish (4:14, 16). A sleepless king hears the page about Mordecai, and Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for him. A decree that cannot be revoked is answered by another; on the day chosen for the Jews' destruction the reverse occurred (9:1), and Haman's lots give their name to Purim.

The book is honest about hard things. Esther eats the king's food and conceals her people where Daniel refused; the narrator records it without comment, and God uses a young woman in a situation she did not choose. Chapter 9 records the Jews killing their enemies, framed as defence against those who came to kill them, with no plunder taken. The church is given no such sword (2 Cor 10:4).

And the book points to Christ. Esther going in uncalled to plead for a condemned people is a shadow of the Intercessor who went knowing he would die, through whom we draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Heb 4:16). Haman's gallows, raised for the righteous man, held the guilty; on the cross the Righteous One bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet 2:24). A sentence that could not be revoked was answered by another word: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). And of those who serve the Son, the Father will honor him (John 12:26).

The book ends with Mordecai second to the king, seeking his people's welfare (10:3). God is not named in the last sentence either. His hand has been on every page.

1.title: The Banquet, the Queen, and the Empty Throne
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces,<sup>2</sup>in those days when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel,<sup>3</sup>in the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media and the nobles and governors of the provinces were before him,<sup>4</sup>while he showed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days.<sup>5</sup>And when these days were completed, the king gave for all the people present in Susa the citadel, both great and small, a feast lasting for seven days in the court of the garden of the king's palace.<sup>6</sup>There were white cotton curtains and violet hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars, and also couches of gold and silver on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stones.<sup>7</sup>Drinks were served in golden vessels, vessels of different kinds, and the royal wine was lavished according to the bounty of the king.<sup>8</sup>And drinking was according to this edict: "There is no compulsion." For the king had given orders to all the staff of his palace to do as each man desired.<sup>9</sup>Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus.<sup>10</sup>On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus,<sup>11</sup>to bring Queen Vashti before the king with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty, for she was lovely to look at.<sup>12</sup>But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him.<sup>13</sup>Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times (for this was the king's procedure toward all who were versed in law and judgment,<sup>14</sup>the men next to him being Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom):<sup>15</sup>"According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti, because she has not performed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"<sup>16</sup>Then Memucan said in the presence of the king and the officials, "Not only against the king has Queen Vashti done wrong, but also against all the officials and all the peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.<sup>17</sup>For the queen's behavior will be made known to all women, causing them to look at their husbands with contempt, since they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.'<sup>18</sup>This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's behavior will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty.<sup>19</sup>If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it may not be repealed, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she.<sup>20</sup>So when the decree made by the king is proclaimed throughout all his kingdom, for it is vast, all women will give honor to their husbands, high and low alike."<sup>21</sup>This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan proposed.<sup>22</sup>He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, that every man be master in his own household and speak according to the language of his people.
1.overview: Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, 486-465 BC), ruler of 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia, displays the riches of his royal glory for 180 days in Susa, then feasts the whole city for seven days, while Queen Vashti feasts the women (vv. 1-9). Merry with wine, he sends for Vashti to show off her beauty; she refuses, and he is enraged (vv. 10-12). His counsellors turn the refusal into a threat to every husband in the empire; an unrepealable decree removes Vashti and gives her place to another who is better than she, Samuel's words to Saul (1 Sam 15:28), and letters go to every province that every man be master in his own household (vv. 13-22).
1.theology:
God is not named in this chapter, and he is never absent from it. He rules through a drunken king's vanity, a queen's refusal and a counsellor's panic as surely as through a parted sea. The law that cannot be repealed, introduced here, and the Saul-and-Agag words the counsellor borrows are the machinery the rest of the story will run on.

Ahasuerus summons his queen to display her beauty for his glory; Christ gives himself for his bride to make her beautiful (Eph 5:25-27, see on vv. 10-12).
1.examples: The chapter is full of power that turns out hollow. Half a year of display came three years before Xerxes' fleet was lost at Salamis; the king who ruled 127 provinces could not bring his wife across a courtyard; and the empire's whole postal system was set moving to announce that husbands must be respected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Riches of His Royal Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahasuerus holds court in Susa (vv. 1-2), feasts his officials and army for 180 days to show the riches of his royal glory (vv. 3-4), then gives all Susa a seven-day feast in the palace garden among gold couches and golden cups (vv. 5-8). Queen Vashti gives a feast for the women (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The book opens on the most powerful man in the world at the height of his glory, and teaches the reader to look for the hand the story does not name.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces, in those days when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa, the citadel, in the third year of his reign he gave a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media and the nobles and governors of the provinces were before him, while he showed the riches of his royal glory and the splendor and pomp of his greatness for many days, 180 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the name the Greeks wrote as Xerxes, the Persian king who reigned from 486 to 465 BC, over an empire from the Indus to the upper Nile. His palace in Susa is the one where, a generation later, a Jew named Nehemiah would hand his son the wine (Neh 1:1; 2:1).

In this book no one is said to pray. The reader has to learn to see a hand in the timing of a feast, a refusal and a sleepless night, which is how ordinary believers live most of their days, among events that do not explain themselves.

The display lasted half a year. The third year of Xerxes was 483 BC, and within three years his invasion of Greece had met disaster when his fleet was beaten at Salamis (480 BC). Many think the 180 days were partly a gathering of the empire's leaders to plan that campaign. The glory on display was not as solid as it looked.
verseByVerse.note: Susa was the Persian kings' winter capital, in modern Iran.

verseByVerse.quote: And when these days were completed, the king gave for all the people present in Susa the citadel, both great and small, a feast lasting for seven days in the court of the garden of the king's palace. There were white cotton curtains and violet hangings fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rods and marble pillars, and also couches of gold and silver on a mosaic pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stones. Drinks were served in golden vessels, vessels of different kinds, and the royal wine was lavished according to the bounty of the king. And drinking was according to this edict: "There is no compulsion." For the king had given orders to all the staff of his palace to do as each man desired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator lingers on the furnishings as if walking us through a showroom: silver rods, marble pillars, couches of gold and silver on a pavement of porphyry and mother-of-pearl. Everyone in the city, great and small, is drinking from gold.

Even the drinking is by royal decree. This is a book full of decrees, in which what the king desires is done. And there is irony here: at this feast no one is compelled to drink; in a few verses one person will be compelled to come, and will not.

The Hebrew word for feast comes about twenty times in this short book. Kings decide things at feasts in Esther, usually with wine in them, and the whole story will turn on two small feasts given by a queen.

verseByVerse.quote: Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus.
verseByVerse.commentary: One verse, and a queen with a household and a feast of her own, in the palace that belonged to King Ahasuerus. Everything in this world belongs to the king: the palace, the cups, the provinces and, he assumes, the queen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he sends for Queen Vashti to show her beauty to the peoples and the princes (vv. 10-11). She refuses, and his anger burns within him (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The book does not tell us why she refused; it tells us that an empty throne was the result.

verseByVerse.quote: On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus, to bring Queen Vashti before the king with her royal crown, in order to show the peoples and the princes her beauty, for she was lovely to look at. But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A week of wine, a hall full of men, and the king sends for his wife to be looked at, displayed like the golden cups: one more possession, the finest one. Lovely to look at is exactly what will be said of Esther in the next chapter (2:7). In this court, that is what a woman is for.

The narrator does not tell us why she refused. He neither praises Vashti nor blames her, and we should not fill the silence with our own story. But he has shown us the summons, and the reader can see it for what it is.

A reader may be living inside a marriage where what is asked of her is degrading. Scripture's call to wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord, sits directly beside the call to husbands: love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:22, 25). A summons to be paraded before drunken men is the opposite of that love, and no one is bound to obey a command to shame or sin: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Here is the contrast the whole Bible draws. This king called for his queen to show off her beauty for his own glory. There is another King who gave himself for his bride, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:27), and whose feast is the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9). When the wine ran out at a village wedding, he quietly made more and manifested his glory (John 2:11). One king uses his bride to display his glory. The other spends his glory to make his bride beautiful.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — So That It May Not Be Repealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king asks his wise men what the law requires (vv. 13-15). Memucan warns that every wife will now despise her husband and proposes an unrepealable decree giving Vashti's place to another (vv. 16-20). Letters go to every province, that every man be master in his own household (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The decree is a comedy here, where it deposes a queen; the same kind of law will be a terror in chapter 3.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the wise men who knew the times (for this was the king's procedure toward all who were versed in law and judgment, the men next to him being Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom): "According to the law, what is to be done to Queen Vashti, because she has not performed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven named princes, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom: the kind of council of seven that sent Ezra to Jerusalem under the next king (Ezra 7:14). The ruler of the world, publicly refused, turns to his lawyers.

There is comedy in it, and the narrator means us to hear it. The most powerful man on earth cannot manage his own household without a meeting of the cabinet.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Memucan said in the presence of the king and the officials, "Not only against the king has Queen Vashti done wrong, but also against all the officials and all the peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. For the queen's behavior will be made known to all women, causing them to look at their husbands with contempt, since they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, and she did not come.' This very day the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen's behavior will say the same to all the king's officials, and there will be contempt and wrath in plenty. If it please the king, let a royal order go out from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes so that it may not be repealed, that Vashti is never again to come before King Ahasuerus. And let the king give her royal position to another who is better than she. So when the decree made by the king is proclaimed throughout all his kingdom, for it is vast, all women will give honor to their husbands, high and low alike."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Memucan turns one refusal into a threat to every husband in the empire. This very day, he says, the noblewomen will be saying it at dinner.

Here, for the first time, is the rule the whole plot will hang on. The law of the Medes and Persians could not be changed even by the king who made it (Dan 6:8, 15). In chapter 3 it will sentence a nation to death, and even the king will not be able to take it back (8:8).

Another who is better than she. When Saul spared Agag king of the Amalekites, Samuel told him, The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (1 Sam 15:28). A Persian lawyer who had almost certainly never heard of Samuel uses the same words. And the Saul and Agag story is about to be played again: Mordecai will be introduced as a Benjaminite, son of Kish (2:5), and his enemy as Haman the Agagite (3:1). The narrator never says God is arranging things. He lets the words say it.

verseByVerse.quote: This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan proposed. He sent letters to all the royal provinces, to every province in its own script and to every people in its own language, that every man be master in his own household and speak according to the language of his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole imperial post, in every script from India to Ethiopia, is set moving to announce that husbands are in charge: the most powerful state on earth making itself ridiculous. A law can depose a queen; it cannot make anyone honour anyone. Respect cannot be decreed, and love less still.

Remember those couriers. The same postal system will carry a decree of death to every province in chapter 3, and a decree of life in chapter 8. And the throne beside the king is now empty. Nobody in Susa that night was thinking about the Jews. Someone was.

2.title: The Girl From Exile: Esther Comes to the Throne
2.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her.<sup>2</sup>Then the king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king.<sup>3</sup>And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to the harem in Susa the citadel, under custody of Hegai, the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women. Let their cosmetics be given them.<sup>4</sup>And let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti." This pleased the king, and he did so.<sup>5</sup>Now there was a Jew in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,<sup>6</sup>who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the captives carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away.<sup>7</sup>He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was lovely to look at, and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.<sup>8</sup>So when the king's order and his edict were proclaimed, and when many young women were gathered in Susa the citadel in custody of Hegai, Esther also was taken into the king's palace and put in custody of Hegai, who had charge of the women.<sup>9</sup>And the young woman pleased him and won his favor. And he quickly provided her with her cosmetics and her portion of food, and with seven chosen young women from the king's palace, and advanced her and her young women to the best place in the harem.<sup>10</sup>Esther had not made known her people or kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known.<sup>11</sup>And every day Mordecai walked in front of the court of the harem to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.<sup>12</sup>Now when the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, after being twelve months under the regulations for the women, since this was the regular period of their beautifying, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women—<sup>13</sup>when the young woman went in to the king in this way, she was given whatever she desired to take with her from the harem to the king's palace.<sup>14</sup>In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second harem in custody of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again, unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.<sup>15</sup>When the turn came for Esther the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, who had charge of the women, advised. Now Esther was winning favor in the eyes of all who saw her.<sup>16</sup>And when Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal palace, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign,<sup>17</sup>the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.<sup>18</sup>Then the king gave a great feast for all his officials and servants; it was Esther's feast. He also granted a remission of taxes to the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.<sup>19</sup>Now when the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.<sup>20</sup>Esther had not made known her kindred or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him.<sup>21</sup>In those days, as Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.<sup>22</sup>And this came to the knowledge of Mordecai, and he told it to Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in the name of Mordecai.<sup>23</sup>When the affair was investigated and found to be so, the men were both hanged on the gallows. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king.
2.overview: With Vashti deposed, beautiful young women are gathered from every province into the king's harem, and whoever pleases him will be queen (vv. 1-4). Mordecai, a Benjaminite whose family names are Saul's, has raised his orphaned cousin Hadassah, Esther, as his own daughter (vv. 5-7). Taken to the harem, she wins Hegai's favour and on Mordecai's orders keeps her people secret (vv. 8-11). After a year of preparation each girl spends one night with the king (vv. 12-14); in Xerxes' seventh year the king loves Esther above all and crowns her queen (vv. 15-18). Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king's life; the deed is recorded in the royal chronicles, unrewarded (vv. 19-23).
2.theology: God is still unnamed, and his hand is everywhere: an orphan placed in the palace, favour given as the LORD once gave it to Joseph (Gen 39:21), a good deed filed in an archive to be found at the right moment. He works through people in situations they did not choose and do not always handle well, without approving everything they do. And nothing done for him is lost, even when no one says thank you.
2.examples: Small details carry the chapter: a cousin who walked past the harem wall every day to ask how she was, a girl who took only what she was advised to take, and a man who saved the king's life and got nothing but a line in the annals.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Let the Young Woman Who Pleases the King Be Queen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When his anger has cooled, the king remembers Vashti (v. 1). His young men propose that beautiful young virgins be gathered from every province into the harem at Susa, and let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti (vv. 2-4).
verseByVerse.theology: The empire begins to replace a queen by gathering young women from 127 provinces like tribute.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had abated, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what had been decreed against her. Then the king's young men who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for the king. And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to the harem in Susa the citadel, under custody of Hegai, the king's eunuch, who is in charge of the women. Let their cosmetics be given them. And let the young woman who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti." This pleased the king, and he did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wine has worn off and the anger with it. He remembers her. But the decree cannot be repealed: the law that was supposed to show the king's power has trapped him.

Call it what it is: girls taken from their families in every province of the empire, brought to the palace as a king's selection. The narrator does not stop to condemn it, but he does not dress it up either. And into the middle of this he is about to set a Jewish orphan.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai's orphaned cousin is taken into the harem, wins favour and keeps her people secret (vv. 5-11). After a year of preparation each young woman has one night with the king (vv. 12-14), and the king loved Esther more than all the women and made her queen (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The favor and grace Esther wins in this chapter are given by someone. Esther never says who.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a Jew in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite, who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the captives carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away. He was bringing up Hadassah, that is Esther, the daughter of his uncle, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was lovely to look at, and when her father and her mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every Israelite reader would hear those names. There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish: that is how the story of Saul begins (1 Sam 9:1). Shimei was the man of Saul's house who cursed David on his flight from Absalom (2 Sam 16:5). Mordecai comes from the family of Israel's first king. Keep that in mind until the next chapter introduces his enemy.

Jeconiah went into exile in 597 BC (2 Kgs 24:12), and Esther is taken to the king in 479 BC (v. 16): 118 years. So the one carried away must be the family's ancestor, most naturally Kish, and not Mordecai himself. Mordecai is the great-grandson of the exile, born in Persia, a Jew who never went home.

She has two names. Hadassah is Hebrew for myrtle, the tree Isaiah promised would grow instead of the brier (Isa 55:13); Esther is her Persian name, perhaps meaning star. A Jewish girl with a Persian name, an orphan brought up by her cousin as his daughter.

Many readers know what it is to lose a parent, or to have been raised by someone who did not have to take them in. Mordecai's kindness is a small picture of a larger one: God sent his Son to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (Gal 4:5), and the Son promised, I will not leave you as orphans (John 14:18).
verseByVerse.note: Kish and Shimei are both names from Saul’s family.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the king's order and his edict were proclaimed, and when many young women were gathered in Susa the citadel in custody of Hegai, Esther also was taken into the king's palace and put in custody of Hegai, who had charge of the women. And the young woman pleased him and won his favor. And he quickly provided her with her cosmetics and her portion of food, and with seven chosen young women from the king's palace, and advanced her and her young women to the best place in the harem. Esther had not made known her people or kindred, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known. And every day Mordecai walked in front of the court of the harem to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb was taken is passive. She did not enter a contest; she was collected.

The word for favor here is hesed, the Old Testament's great word for God's steadfast love. A eunuch in a pagan harem shows it to a Jewish girl, and the text does not say why.

Here is a hard question. Esther eats the king's food, where Daniel, taken to a pagan court a century earlier, resolved that he would not defile himself with the king's food (Dan 1:8). She keeps her people secret, and in time she will spend a night with a pagan king. The narrator makes no comment. Esther is not presented as a model of Daniel's resistance. She is a young woman in a situation she did not choose, doing what the people around her advise. And God does not wait for his people to handle everything well before he uses them. That is not permission to compromise. It is mercy for those who already have.

Why Mordecai insisted on silence, we are not told; the next chapter will show what one man in power could do to a people he hated. He could not get her out, so every day he walked past the wall that held her, asking for news: a picture of helpless love that will not stop caring.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, after being twelve months under the regulations for the women, since this was the regular period of their beautifying, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women— when the young woman went in to the king in this way, she was given whatever she desired to take with her from the harem to the king's palace. In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second harem in custody of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again, unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A whole year of preparation led to one night. For every girl not chosen, what followed was her life: the second harem, a concubine for ever, never to marry, never to go home, waiting to be called by name and almost certainly never called. The narrator states it in one flat sentence. The cruelty is in the flatness.

Some readers will find this chapter painful because something like it happened to them: they were taken, used, or treated as a thing to be enjoyed and set aside. Scripture does not blame Esther or the other girls for what was done to them, and neither should we; the shame belongs to those who took them. Abuse is never acceptable, and anyone in danger now should seek safety at once and tell someone who can help. And the gospel's King is the opposite of this one. He does not choose one bride for her beauty and leave the rest waiting for ever: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: When the turn came for Esther the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai the king's eunuch, who had charge of the women, advised. Now Esther was winning favor in the eyes of all who saw her. And when Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal palace, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign, the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti. Then the king gave a great feast for all his officials and servants; it was Esther's feast. He also granted a remission of taxes to the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the moment she goes in, the narrator gives the orphan's father a name: Esther the daughter of Abihail. She is somebody's daughter. Every other girl could take whatever she desired (v. 13); Esther took only what she was advised to take. She did not grasp.

The feast of chapter 1 was in the third year. Four years have passed: the years in which Xerxes led his armies into Greece and came home defeated. The king who sat down with Esther had lost a war.

Grace and favor are the language Genesis uses of Joseph in prison: the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor (Gen 39:21). In Genesis the giver is named. In Esther he is not. That is how this whole book talks about God.

It was Esther's feast. An orphan of the exile, with no family but a cousin at the gate, wears the crown of Persia, and nobody in the palace knows she is a Jew.

Did Esther sin by going to the king? She was taken, not a volunteer (v. 8), and the book does not praise the harem or make it a model. Marrying a pagan king went against the spirit of the law (Deut 7:3–4), but Esther did not choose it, and God worked through even this to save his people. Scripture records it honestly, as it records Joseph’s Egyptian marriage, without approving every circumstance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — Recorded in the Book of the Chronicles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai sits at the king's gate, and Esther still keeps her people secret (vv. 19-20). Mordecai reports a plot against the king through Esther; the men are hanged, and the deed is recorded in the chronicles (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The deed goes into a book and is forgotten by everyone but the One the book never names.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the virgins were gathered together the second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. Esther had not made known her kindred or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him.
verseByVerse.commentary: A second gathering of girls, after Esther had been crowned: the harem went on filling. Esther's crown did not make her secure, and in chapter 4 she will say she has not been called to the king for thirty days (4:11). The gate was where officials sat and business was done; Mordecai had some post in the king's service. Queen of Persia, Esther still did what her cousin told her, and that habit of trust between them is what the whole deliverance will run on.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, as Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. And this came to the knowledge of Mordecai, and he told it to Queen Esther, and Esther told the king in the name of Mordecai. When the affair was investigated and found to be so, the men were both hanged on the gallows. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the presence of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two of the men who guarded the door of the king's rooms plotted to murder him, and Mordecai's warning reached the king in the name of Mordecai.

The word for gallows is simply wood, a tree; it will appear again, fifty cubits high, in chapter 5. And the chapter ends on a book. Mordecai saved the king's life and received no reward, no promotion, not even thanks. A clerk wrote a line in the annals, and everybody forgot.

Anyone who has done a costly good thing and seen it vanish without a word of thanks knows this sentence. In God's world nothing recorded is lost: a book of remembrance was written before him (Mal 3:16). The Persian clerk thought he was filing a routine report. He was placing the most important page of the story exactly where a sleepless king would one day find it (6:1-2).

3.title: The Decree of Death: Haman's Plot Against the Jews
3.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, and advanced him and set his throne above all the officials who were with him.<sup>2</sup>And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage.<sup>3</sup>Then the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you transgress the king's command?"<sup>4</sup>And when they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, in order to see whether Mordecai's words would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.<sup>5</sup>And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury.<sup>6</sup>But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. So, as they had made known to him the people of Mordecai, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.<sup>7</sup>In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.<sup>8</sup>Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so that it is not to the king's profit to tolerate them.<sup>9</sup>If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will pay 10,000 talents of silver into the hands of those who have charge of the king's business, that they may put it into the king's treasuries."<sup>10</sup>So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews.<sup>11</sup>And the king said to Haman, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you."<sup>12</sup>Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an edict, according to all that Haman commanded, was written to the king's satraps and to the governors over all the provinces and to the officials of all the peoples, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.<sup>13</sup>Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with instruction to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.<sup>14</sup>A copy of the document was to be issued as a decree in every province by proclamation to all the peoples to be ready for that day.<sup>15</sup>The couriers went out hurriedly by order of the king, and the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
3.overview: The king promotes Haman the Agagite above all his officials, and everyone bows to him except Mordecai, a Jew of the family of Kish (vv. 1-4). Haman, enraged, decides to destroy not Mordecai alone but every Jew in the empire (vv. 5-6). Lots (Pur) are cast for the day, and the lot falls eleven months away (v. 7). Haman tells the king of an unnamed people who do not keep the king's laws and offers a fortune in silver; the king hands him the signet ring and the people (vv. 8-11). The decree goes out to kill all Jews, young and old, on one day (vv. 12-14). The king and Haman sit down to drink while Susa is thrown into confusion (v. 15).
3.theology:
The ancient war with Amalek, left unfinished by Saul (1 Sam 15), returns: an Agagite turns the sentence once given against Amalek on the people of God. Behind it is the oldest enmity of all, the attempt to destroy the people from whom the Messiah would come.

Haman cast lots for the day of death, but the lots were not his to govern. The decree written on the eve of Passover would be undone, and its lots would name the feast of deliverance.
3.examples: The chapter turns on injustice and indifference. The man who saved the king got nothing, while Haman was promoted for nothing. Haman never named the people he wanted destroyed, and the king gave them away without asking who they were, his own queen among them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Mordecai Did Not Bow Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everyone at the king's gate bows to Haman except Mordecai, who tells them he is a Jew (vv. 1-4). Haman, filled with fury, sets out to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The son of Kish will not bow to the Agagite, and an old war comes back to life in the Persian court.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, and advanced him and set his throne above all the officials who were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things: after Mordecai saved the king's life and received nothing (2:23). The man who deserved honour is left at the gate; a man of whom we are told nothing is raised above everyone. That is how the world often looks. The book is not going to leave it there.

For a Jewish reader, the one word Agagite is enough. Agag was king of the Amalekites, who fell on Israel's stragglers in the wilderness, when you were faint and weary (Deut 25:18), and of whom God said, The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exod 17:16). Saul, son of Kish, was sent to finish that war and spared Agag (1 Sam 15:9). More than five hundred years later Mordecai, son of Kish, meets Haman, almost certainly of the line of Agag.
verseByVerse.note: An Agagite: probably a descendant of Agag, king of the Amalekites, whom Saul spared.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the king's servants who were at the king's gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage. Then the king's servants who were at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you transgress the king's command?" And when they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they told Haman, in order to see whether Mordecai's words would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why not? Israelites bowed to kings and great men without sin: David bowed to Saul with his face to the ground (1 Sam 24:8), and Abraham bowed to the Hittites (Gen 23:7). The only reason the text gives is in verse 4: he had told them that he was a Jew. A Jew, son of Kish, would not bow to an Agagite. Whether there was more to it, divine honours claimed by Haman or simply the old enmity, the narrator does not say, and he does not say that Mordecai was wrong.

Day after day, the pressure of colleagues: everybody else does it; why won't you? Most of us know that kind of pressure at work. Mordecai stood in it quietly, and it cost him far more than he could have guessed.

That is the hard part of this chapter for a believer. Faithfulness does not always make things safer, and sometimes it puts others at risk too: Mordecai's refusal would bring a death sentence on every Jew in the empire. Jesus told his disciples to expect such things: If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you (John 15:18). He went that way first, and he does not send his people into it alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury. But he disdained to lay hands on Mordecai alone. So, as they had made known to him the people of Mordecai, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus.
verseByVerse.commentary: One man would not bow, and a whole people is sentenced. Killing Mordecai alone was beneath Haman's dignity; a grievance that size needed a nation to satisfy it. That has been the logic of many a genocide since: a personal hatred given the power of a state. And behind this hatred the Bible sees the oldest war of all, the enmity between the serpent and the offspring of the woman (Gen 3:15). To destroy all the Jews would have been to destroy the family from which the Messiah was to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — To Destroy, to Kill, and to Annihilate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lot falls on Adar (v. 7). Haman buys the king's consent to destroy a certain people scattered abroad (vv. 8-11), the decree goes out in every language (vv. 12-14), and the king and Haman sit down to drink (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The Jews of the empire would hear their death sentence as they prepared to remember their deliverance from Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first month, which is the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur (that is, they cast lots) before Haman day after day; and they cast it month after month till the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The twelfth year is five years after Esther was crowned (2:16). And the month is Nisan, the month of Passover, when every Jewish household remembered the night God struck Egypt and brought his people out. In that month an Agagite sat casting lots to find the day to wipe them out.

Pur is a foreign word, explained in the verse itself, and it will give the festival its name: Purim, Lots (9:24-26). Haman consulted chance to choose the day of death, and the lot fell eleven months away, time for everything that follows. Proverbs had already said who governs the dice: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33).
verseByVerse.note: Pur is the word for “lot” — the origin of the name Purim.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws, so that it is not to the king's profit to tolerate them. If it please the king, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will pay 10,000 talents of silver into the hands of those who have charge of the king's business, that they may put it into the king's treasuries."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen to how it is done. He never names them: a certain people. He mixes truth with lies: their laws were different; they kept a Sabbath, ate differently and worshipped one God. But they do not keep the king's laws was false, except for one man at one gate refusing one bow. And he closes with the argument that moves kings: it does not pay to tolerate them.

Christians should recognise the charge. The church too is a people scattered abroad; Peter writes to believers as elect exiles of the Dispersion (1 Pet 1:1). Its laws are different, and it has often been accused of not keeping the king's.

Haman was ready to pay a fortune out of his own estate to see his grudge satisfied.
verseByVerse.note: Ten thousand talents of silver is about 340 metric tons (a talent was about 75 pounds or 34 kilograms, ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. And the king said to Haman, "The money is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ring made a document the king's own, and with it went the power of life and death over millions. And the narrator gives Haman his title for the first time: the enemy of the Jews.

The king does not ask who this people is, or what they have done. He seems to wave the silver away, though the sum is remembered later (4:7; 7:4), and simply hands a nation to the man who hates them. It is not even cruelty; it is indifference, which has killed as many as cruelty ever has. And his own queen was one of the people he had just given away.
verseByVerse.note: The signet ring sealed royal decrees with the king’s authority.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and an edict, according to all that Haman commanded, was written to the king's satraps and to the governors over all the provinces and to the officials of all the peoples, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring. Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with instruction to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all Jews, young and old, women and children, in one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, and to plunder their goods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thirteenth day of the first month. The Passover lambs were killed on the fourteenth (Exod 12:6). The decree of death was written on the eve of Passover, and it would reach Jewish homes as they gathered to remember that God had once struck down the firstborn of their oppressors and spared theirs.

Three verbs, so that no one could misunderstand. And the list, young and old, women and children, is the list Saul was given against Amalek: kill both man and woman, child and infant (1 Sam 15:3). Saul did not carry out that sentence on Agag's people; now an Agagite writes it against the people of Saul. That old sentence troubles readers, and it needs a word. It was God's judgment, once and on one nation, against a people who had made a practice of preying on the weak and weary (Deut 25:17-19), given to Israel as the Judge's instrument and never as a pattern for anyone else. Haman's decree is the opposite: a man's private hatred dressed up as law. The plunder was the bribe: whoever killed a Jew could keep his house. The postal system that carried the letters about Vashti now carries a death sentence to every Jewish family from India to Ethiopia, and they have eleven months to wait for it.

verseByVerse.quote: A copy of the document was to be issued as a decree in every province by proclamation to all the peoples to be ready for that day. The couriers went out hurriedly by order of the king, and the decree was issued in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In every town in the empire it was nailed up for the neighbours to read: be ready.

One sentence holds two scenes: inside, two powerful men with their cups, business concluded; outside, a city that did not understand what had just happened, for even pagan Susa was shaken. It is the picture of the powerful condemning the innocent and sitting down content. The Gospels have another such scene: when the innocent Son of God had been sent from one ruler to another, Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day (Luke 23:12).

But the decree can only name a day eleven months away. It cannot stop the One who governs every lot from working in those months. The Jews of Susa went to bed under a law that could not be repealed, not knowing that a Jew was wearing the queen's crown, put there five years before the danger existed.

4.title: For Such a Time as This: The Hinge of the Book
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and he cried out with a loud and bitter cry.<sup>2</sup>He went up to the entrance of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.<sup>3</sup>And in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting, and many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes.<sup>4</sup>When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.<sup>5</sup>Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, who had been appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was.<sup>6</sup>Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city in front of the king's gate,<sup>7</sup>and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.<sup>8</sup>Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her and command her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people.<sup>9</sup>And Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.<sup>10</sup>Then Esther spoke to Hathach and commanded him to go to Mordecai and say,<sup>11</sup>"All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is but one law—to be put to death, except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter so that he may live. But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days."<sup>12</sup>And they told Mordecai what Esther had said.<sup>13</sup>Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews.<sup>14</sup>For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"<sup>15</sup>Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai,<sup>16</sup>"Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish."<sup>17</sup>Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him.
4.overview: When Mordecai learns of the decree he puts on sackcloth and cries aloud through the city, and in every province the Jews mourn with fasting (vv. 1-3). Through her servant Hathach he tells Esther to plead for her people (vv. 4-9). She answers that to go to the king uncalled is death (vv. 10-12); Mordecai replies that the palace will not save her, and who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this? (vv. 13-14). Esther asks the Jews of Susa to fast for her, and resolves to go (vv. 15-17).
4.theology:
God's purpose to preserve his people is certain, and the people he places are still called to act; neither truth cancels the other. The chapter never names God and is full of him: sackcloth, fasting and the who knows of the prophets are the language of a people crying to the only one who can reverse a sentence.

Esther risks death to plead for a condemned people. Christ went knowing he would die, bore the sentence, and now holds the sceptre out to all who come through him (see on vv. 15-16).
4.examples: Esther's first instinct was to send Mordecai clothes, as if the trouble could be dressed away. By the end of the chapter the girl who had always obeyed him is giving him his orders, and walking toward a throne that may kill her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Loud and Bitter Cry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai mourns at the king's gate, and the Jews of every province with him (vv. 1-3). Esther sends him clothes, which he refuses (v. 4); he sends her a copy of the decree and tells her to plead for her people (vv. 5-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A whole people in sackcloth, fasting, crying out: in a book that never mentions prayer, it is hard to read this as anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: When Mordecai learned all that had been done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city, and he cried out with a loud and bitter cry. He went up to the entrance of the king's gate, for no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is no private grief. He goes into the middle of the city in sackcloth and ashes, crying aloud, and everyone in Susa can see what the king's decree means.

And the words may be old ones. Many readers hear in a loud and bitter cry the cry of Esau when Jacob had taken his blessing: he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry (Gen 27:34). Amalek was Esau's grandson (Gen 36:12). Now an Agagite, of Amalek's line, has drawn the same cry out of a son of Jacob.

The Persian palace had a rule: no grief inside. The king was not to be troubled by mourning. So Mordecai goes as far as he is allowed and cries at the door.

Set that beside the throne the Christian approaches. There, mourners are not kept at the gate; Christ calls them blessed: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:4). He came to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning (Isa 61:3). No one needs to change out of sackcloth to come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting, and many of them lay in sackcloth and ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind the couriers, town after town, the Jews put on sackcloth. Picture a Jewish family in a village a thousand miles from Susa reading the notice on the wall: on a day in Adar, eleven months from now, your neighbours may kill you and keep your house.

Prayer is not mentioned; it does not need to be. Fasting and weeping are the words of Joel's call to a people under judgment: return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning (Joel 2:12). The book shows a whole nation doing what people do when they have no one left to cry to except God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them. Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs, who had been appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why it was. Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city in front of the king's gate,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther does not yet know about the decree. She only knows that Mordecai is in sackcloth at the gate, and her first instinct is to get him into proper clothes: fix the outside, and perhaps the trouble will go away. He will not have it. The sackcloth is the message. As Joel said, the point is to rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:13), and no change of clothes can deal with a decree of death.

From here the whole conversation passes through a go-between. The queen cannot go out; Mordecai cannot come in. Every word between them is carried across the courtyard by a servant.

verseByVerse.quote: and Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews. Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, that he might show it to Esther and explain it to her and command her to go to the king to beg his favor and plead with him on behalf of her people. And Hathach went and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai knew the exact sum (3:9); a man at the king's gate hears things. He wants Esther to know exactly what her people are worth to Haman.

For years Mordecai had told her to keep her people secret (2:10, 20). Now he tells her to plead for them: the secret that protected her has become the thing she must risk. And plead is the language of intercession: a queen standing between a king and a condemned people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — For Such a Time as This
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther explains the law of the inner court (vv. 10-12). Mordecai answers that silence will not save her, that deliverance will come from another place, and that she may have come to the kingdom for this (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Two convictions in one breath: God's people will be delivered whatever Esther does; and Esther is where she is for a reason. Neither cancels the other. God does not need her, and he has placed her.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther spoke to Hathach and commanded him to go to Mordecai and say, "All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is but one law—to be put to death, except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter so that he may live. But as for me, I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days." And they told Mordecai what Esther had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esther is not making excuses; she is telling Mordecai the truth about the palace. To walk into the inner court uncalled is to walk into your own execution, unless the king, in that moment, lifts his golden sceptre toward you.

And she has had thirty days with no summons. The harem had gone on filling after she was crowned (2:19). She has no reason to think the king still wants to see her, and every reason to remember what happened to the last queen who crossed him.

Many readers know the feeling: knowing what ought to be done and exactly what it may cost. Esther's hesitation is not cowardice. It is honesty about the price, and that is where real courage has to start.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai takes away her last hiding place. The decree says all Jews; the palace walls will not stop it, and sooner or later someone will tell Haman who the queen's cousin is. Silence will only mean that she dies later, having done nothing.

That is still the truth about silence. A believer who hides in a comfortable place while the people of God are in danger may keep his comfort for a while. He has not escaped.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things, and both are true. First: relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place. Mordecai is sure the people will survive, though he does not say how. God had sworn that Israel would last as long as the sun and moon (Jer 31:35-36), and centuries later another Benjaminite would ask, has God rejected his people? By no means! (Rom 11:1). Later Jewish writers used the Place as a name for God, and some hear it here; either way, the deliverance does not depend on Esther.

And you and your father's house will perish. Her father's name has been given only once: Esther the daughter of Abihail (2:15). As far as we are told, she is all that is left of that house.

Second: who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this? She is an orphan made queen, crowned five years before anyone had heard of Haman's plan. Mordecai looks at the strange road that brought her to the throne and asks whether this was what it was for.

And who knows is the prophets' phrase for a people under sentence: Who knows whether he will not turn and relent (Joel 2:14). The king of Nineveh, in ashes, ordered a fast with the same words: Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish (Jonah 3:9). Sackcloth, ashes, fasting, who knows, perish: every one is in this chapter. The name of God is not, but the reader of the prophets can hear whom they are hoping in.

Here is a question every believer can put to himself. Where has God put you: which family, which job, which room you can walk into that others cannot? It is not an accident. There may be a moment for which it was all arranged. And the One who placed you does not send you in your own strength: his Spirit lives in those who belong to him, and when we fail to speak, as all of us have, Christ has already been faithful in our place, and the way back is confession and his mercy (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — If I Perish, I Perish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther asks the Jews of Susa to fast with her for three days, and then she will go to the king (vv. 15-16). Mordecai does as she ordered (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: She goes to the throne not knowing whether she will live, and asks her people to stand with her as she goes.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai, "Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my young women will also fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She does not go alone. She asks her people to fast for her, and she and her maids will fast with them: three days without food or water, the Jewish community of Susa and a queen's household together. It is prayer in everything but the word. And if the fast began as soon as the news came, it fell across Passover, for the decree had been written on the eve of that feast (3:12). The Jews of Susa may have spent that Passover not eating the lamb but fasting.

She does not say she will not perish, which would be bravado, or that she hopes she will not, which would be wishful thinking. She will go, and what happens is not in her hands. That is the shape of courage for a believer: not certainty of the outcome, but willingness to act and leave the outcome with God.

Though it is against the law. She breaks the king's law deliberately, because keeping it would mean standing by while her people were killed. Scripture honours that kind of disobedience: Moses' parents hid their baby and they were not afraid of the king's edict (Heb 11:23). A believer may have to break a human rule to keep a greater duty. What he may not do is pretend the rule does not exist; Esther names it, and accepts the price in advance.

And it points to a greater scene. In a garden outside Jerusalem another intercessor faced the cost of standing for his people and prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). Esther went in not knowing whether she would die. Jesus went knowing all that would happen to him (John 18:4), and he did die, under the sentence that was ours. That is why, for those who belong to him, the sceptre is always held out: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Mordecai then went away and did everything as Esther had ordered him.
verseByVerse.commentary: A small sentence, and a reversal. In chapter 2 Esther obeyed Mordecai just as when she was brought up by him (2:20). Now the girl he raised gives the orders, and he carries them out. From here to the end of the book it is Esther who leads.

5.title: The First Banquet: Grace, Delay, and the Gallows
5.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, in front of the king's quarters, while the king was sitting on his royal throne inside the throne room opposite the entrance to the palace.<sup>2</sup>And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.<sup>3</sup>And the king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom."<sup>4</sup>And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king."<sup>5</sup>Then the king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has asked." So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared.<sup>6</sup>And as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king said to Esther, "What is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."<sup>7</sup>Then Esther answered, "My wish and my request is:<sup>8</sup>If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my wish and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."<sup>9</sup>And Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai.<sup>10</sup>Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and his wife Zeresh.<sup>11</sup>And Haman recounted to them the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions with which the king had honored him, and how he had advanced him above the officials and the servants of the king.<sup>12</sup>Then Haman said, "Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the feast she prepared. And tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king.<sup>13</sup>Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."<sup>14</sup>Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it. Then go joyfully with the king to the feast." This idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
5.overview: On the third day of the fast Esther stands in the inner court; the king holds out the golden sceptre, and she touches it and lives (vv. 1-2). Offered anything up to half the kingdom, she asks only that the king and Haman come to a feast (vv. 3-5). Over the wine he asks again, and she invites them to a second feast the next day (vv. 6-8). Haman leaves delighted, but sees Mordecai at the gate refusing to rise or tremble (vv. 9-10). At home he recounts his riches and honours and says it is all worth nothing while Mordecai sits at the gate; on his wife's advice he has a gallows fifty cubits high built for Mordecai in the morning (vv. 11-14).
5.theology:
Esther approaches the throne uncalled and is received. God works through her courage and through her delay; the extra night she creates is the night he will use. Pride, meanwhile, builds the instrument of its own destruction.

A Persian king offers half his kingdom; the Father is pleased to give his little flock the whole kingdom (Luke 12:32).
5.examples: The same royal offer of half a kingdom bought John the Baptist's head for Herod's dancer and would buy lives for Esther. And Haman's gallows, built in a single night of spite, would be ready on the very morning after the king could not sleep.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king holds out the sceptre to Esther (vv. 1-2). Offered anything, she invites him and Haman to a feast (vv. 3-5), and there she invites them to a second one tomorrow (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: She went in under the sentence of death and lived, and then she did not ask. The one extra night that her delay created is the night on which the whole story turns (6:1).

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king's palace, in front of the king's quarters, while the king was sitting on his royal throne inside the throne room opposite the entrance to the palace. And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the tip of the scepter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She has not eaten or drunk for three days. She puts on her royal robes: she will go to the king as the queen, not as a beggar. And she stands where he can see her, facing the open throne room, and waits for his eyes to fall on her. One look will decide whether she lives.

Third days in Scripture are often days of deliverance. On the third day Abraham saw the mountain where God would provide the lamb (Gen 22:4); on the third day he will raise us up, said Hosea (Hos 6:2). The Christian reader knows the third day on which the one under the sentence of death came out alive (1 Cor 15:4). Esther's third day is a small one and should not be pressed, but it belongs to the same pattern.

The sceptre comes up; she crosses the floor and touches it; she will live. It is the most dangerous walk in the book, and it takes one sentence. For those who belong to Christ, that walk has been made safe for good: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to her, "What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you, even to the half of my kingdom." And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a feast that I have prepared for the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He knows she would not risk her life for nothing. Half of my kingdom is the royal way of saying: ask anything. Five centuries later Herod, at his birthday feast, promised a dancing girl up to half of my kingdom (Mark 6:23), and she asked for the head of John the Baptist. Esther will use the same offer to ask for lives.

What she brings is not a petition but an invitation. She had prepared the feast before she went in: she was planning to live. And she asks for Haman to be there. The man who wrote the decree will be at her table when she asks for it to be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said, "Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther has asked." So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared. And as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king said to Esther, "What is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled." Then Esther answered, "My wish and my request is: If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my wish and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the feast that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king, the queen and the enemy of the Jews drink together, and only one of the three knows what is at stake. The king asks a second time, and the moment has come.

Watch the sentence. She begins, My wish and my request is, and then it becomes another invitation. Did her courage fail at the last moment? Did she judge that the king was not ready, or that one more feast would bind him to her more tightly? The narrator does not say. What he shows is that the delay gave God one night to work with, and that he used it. Many readers know what it is to have meant to say the hard thing and not said it yet. Delay is not always failure, and the God who used Esther's extra night is patient with ours. The question is whether you go back tomorrow. Esther did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Let a Gallows Fifty Cubits High Be Made
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Haman leaves glad, sees Mordecai at the gate and is filled with wrath (v. 9). At home he finds all his honours worth nothing while Mordecai sits there (vv. 10-13), and on his wife's advice he has a gallows made (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The tree Haman raised that night for a righteous Jew will stand in the next chapter with a different body on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai. Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and his wife Zeresh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence takes him from delight to fury. He has dined privately with the king and queen, and one man at the gate who will not stand up for him ruins the whole day. Neither rose nor trembled: Mordecai, under a sentence of death, is not afraid of him.

He controls his face in public and goes home to talk about it. That is how grudges grow.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman recounted to them the splendor of his riches, the number of his sons, all the promotions with which the king had honored him, and how he had advanced him above the officials and the servants of the king. Then Haman said, "Even Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the feast she prepared. And tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king. Yet all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells his own wife and friends what they already know: riches, ten sons (9:7-10), honours, rank. And the crowning boast is the queen's invitation, today and tomorrow. He thinks it is the height of his career. It is the trap.

Yet all of it is worth nothing to me. Everything, minus one man's bow, equals nothing. That is the arithmetic of pride, and it never comes out: there will always be one person who does not bow. Here is a test to run on ourselves: is there one person whose coolness, or success, or refusal to give me my due, spoils everything else I have? If so, the problem is not that person, and the cure is not to try harder at contentment but to look again at what we have been given.

Set Haman's sentence beside Paul's: I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Phil 3:8). Both men count everything as nothing because of one person: Haman, because of a man he hated; Paul, because of the One he loved. The first sentence leads to a gallows. The second leads to Christ.
