verseByVerse.quote: Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it. Then go joyfully with the king to the feast." This idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word for gallows is simply a tree or a stake; Persians often executed by impaling, so the ESV's gallows and hanged may mean a stake rather than a rope. This one would stand higher than the houses, so that all Susa could see what happened to a Jew who would not bow. Mordecai would die before breakfast, and Haman would enjoy the queen's dinner. This idea pleased Haman: the book's favourite phrase, and this time it pleases the one man it should have frightened. Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Prov 16:18).

The gallows was ready by the morning (6:4), and that night was the night the king could not sleep (6:1). Many Christian readers cannot see a tree raised to kill a righteous Jew without thinking of another, raised outside Jerusalem: Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree (Acts 5:30). Haman's tree would be turned on the guilty; that one held the Innocent in the place of the guilty.

6.title: The Night the King Could Not Sleep
6.text: <sup>1</sup>On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king.<sup>2</sup>And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."<sup>4</sup>And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about having Mordecai hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for him.<sup>5</sup>And the king's young men told him, "Haman is there, standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."<sup>6</sup>So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?" And Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"<sup>7</sup>And Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor,<sup>8</sup>let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and the horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown is set.<sup>9</sup>And let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them lead him on the horse through the square of the city, proclaiming before him: 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor.'"<sup>10</sup>Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing that you have mentioned."<sup>11</sup>So Haman took the robes and the horse, and he dressed Mordecai and led him through the square of the city, proclaiming before him, "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor."<sup>12</sup>Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered.<sup>13</sup>And Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him."<sup>14</sup>While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.
6.overview: That night the king cannot sleep and has the royal chronicles read to him; they reach the record of Mordecai's exposure of the plot against his life, and he learns that nothing was ever done for him (vv. 1-3). In the morning Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's hanging, and the king asks him what should be done for the man whom the king delights to honor (vv. 4-6). Thinking it can only be himself, Haman proposes the king's robes and horse and a public proclamation (vv. 7-9), and is ordered to do it all for Mordecai the Jew (vv. 10-11). Haman hurries home mourning, is told he will surely fall, and is hurried away to Esther's feast (vv. 12-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — On That Night the King Could Not Sleep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sleepless king hears the record of Mordecai's good deed (vv. 1-2) and learns that Nothing has been done for him (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The gallows had been ordered and the queen's second feast was hours away. The book never says who kept the king awake.

verseByVerse.quote: On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That night: the night after Esther's first feast, the night Haman had his gallows made. Literally, the king's sleep fled; Daniel records the same of another king of the Persian era, on another night when a Jew's life hung in the balance: Darius spent the night fasting ... and sleep fled from him (Dan 6:18).

Who took the king's sleep? The Hebrew text does not say. When the book was translated into Greek, the translators could not bear the silence and wrote that the Lord took sleep from the king. The Hebrew leaves it unsaid, and trusts the reader. We are not told, and we know. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep (Ps 121:4). The emperor of the world lay awake that night because the Keeper of Israel was awake.

The king's cure for insomnia was to have the court records read aloud. In Hebrew it is the book of remembrances, and the deed filed and forgotten in 2:23 is in it. Malachi spoke of another such book: a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the LORD (Mal 3:16).

Many readers have lain awake with something that will not leave them. The king's sleepless night was not wasted, and neither are ours: the One who does not sleep uses the hours we cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. And the king said, "What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of years of records from 127 provinces, the reader happened to reach this page. It was found written: nobody went looking for it.

The plot was uncovered some time after Esther became queen in the seventh year (2:16, 21); we are now in the twelfth (3:7). For some five years the man who saved the king's life had received nothing. And the reward was delayed until the one morning when it would do the most good: the morning Haman came to ask for his death.

Faithfulness that went unthanked is not lost. God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name (Heb 6:10). The reward may be years in coming, and it will come at the right time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — The Man Whom the King Delights to Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's hanging (vv. 4-5), designs an honour he thinks is for himself (vv. 6-9), and is ordered to give it to Mordecai the Jew (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The gallows was ready, and Haman spent the morning leading Mordecai's horse.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said, "Who is in the court?" Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace to speak to the king about having Mordecai hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for him. And the king's young men told him, "Haman is there, standing in the court." And the king said, "Let him come in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king has spent the night hearing about Mordecai; Haman has spent it planning his death. Both converge on the throne room in the morning. Haman has come early because the gallows is finished, and he wants permission before Esther's feast. Of all the people who might have been in the court at that hour, it is Haman.

He walks in with Mordecai's death in his mouth. He never gets to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Haman came in, and the king said to him, "What should be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?" And Haman said to himself, "Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator lets us hear Haman's thought, Whom would the king delight to honor more than me?, and it is the whole man in one sentence. In the world of the proud there is only one person who deserves honour.

Jesus told of a guest who took the place of honour at a wedding feast and was moved down in front of everyone: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). Haman is about to live out that sentence in the streets of Susa, and Mordecai the second half of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman said to the king, "For the man whom the king delights to honor, let royal robes be brought, which the king has worn, and the horse that the king has ridden, and on whose head a royal crown is set. And let the robes and the horse be handed over to one of the king's most noble officials. Let them dress the man whom the king delights to honor, and let them lead him on the horse through the square of the city, proclaiming before him: 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He does not ask for money or land. He wants to be seen wearing the king: the king's own clothes, on the king's own horse with the royal crest on its head. What Haman craved was not wealth, which he had, but to be treated as royalty in public.

He has designed every detail, including the noble who will lead the horse. He has just written his own job for the worst morning of his life.

A reader of Genesis knows this scene. When Pharaoh raised Joseph, the Hebrew prisoner, he clothed him in garments of fine linen, set him in his chariot, and they called out before him, Bow the knee! (Gen 41:42-43). Another exile in a foreign court, lifted up by a king's robe and a public proclamation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Haman, "Hurry; take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing that you have mentioned." So Haman took the robes and the horse, and he dressed Mordecai and led him through the square of the city, proclaiming before him, "Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to honor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every phrase lands: Mordecai; the Jew; who sits at the king's gate, the very place where he had refused to bow; Leave out nothing. And the king says Mordecai the Jew without a flicker. The decree to kill all the Jews is still posted in every province, and he has not connected the two. He honours a Jew in the morning under a law that will kill him in Adar.

Haman dresses him with his own hands, walks at the horse's head, and shouts the proclamation he had written for himself. The whole city sees it.

There is a King who delights to honour. At the Jordan his voice said of his Son, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17), and after the cross God has highly exalted him (Phil 2:9). That King's delight reaches those who belong to his Son: If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him (John 12:26). The servant who was overlooked will be dressed in robes not his own and brought through the city.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — You Will Surely Fall Before Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai returns to the gate and Haman hurries home in grief (v. 12). His own household foretells his fall (v. 13), and the eunuchs hurry him to Esther's feast (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Even Haman's wife can see which way the story is going.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai returned to the king's gate. But Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The procession ends and he goes back to work. The honour has not gone to his head, and it has not changed his situation: the decree still stands. He returns to his post, as the faithful do.

Covering the head was the gesture of grief and shame; David went up the Mount of Olives weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered (2 Sam 15:30). In chapter 4 it was Mordecai who mourned in the streets. Now the mourning has moved house.

verseByVerse.quote: And Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him, "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The night before, these same people had advised the gallows. This morning they deliver a verdict. In a book that never names God, one of the clearest statements that the Jews cannot be destroyed comes from the enemy's own wife and advisers. They knew the history. God had said to Abraham, I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse (Gen 12:3), and even Persian wise men had noticed that those who set themselves against this nation fell.

Begun to fall ... surely fall. The word comes twice. In the next chapter it will come a third time, when Haman is found falling on the couch where Esther lay (7:8).

verseByVerse.quote: While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried to bring Haman to the feast that Esther had prepared.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has no time to think or recover. Hurry, said the king (v. 10); Haman hurried home (v. 12); now the eunuchs hurried him to the feast. He had been invited as the queen's honoured guest. He goes to her table with his wife's words still in his ears.

That is how the book shows God's hand: not by naming him, but by the timing. Any one of the night's coincidences could be luck; all of them together, on the one night that mattered, make the reader say what the book never says. The Keeper of Israel had not been asleep.

6.theology:
God is unnamed and unmistakable: a king's sleep taken, a page found, a man in the court at the wrong moment, all on the one night that mattered. Faithfulness left unrewarded for years is remembered at the right time.

The proud man is humbled and the humble man exalted, and the King who delights to honour his Son honours those who serve him.
6.examples: The ironies pile up. Haman came to ask for a hanging and was asked to plan an honour, and the king honoured Mordecai the Jew while his decree to kill the Jews still stood.

7.title: The Second Banquet: Esther Speaks, Haman Falls
7.text: <sup>1</sup>So the king and Haman went in to feast with Queen Esther.<sup>2</sup>And on the second day, as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king again said to Esther, "What is your wish, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."<sup>3</sup>Then Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request.<sup>4</sup>For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king."<sup>5</sup>Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?"<sup>6</sup>And Esther said, "A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.<sup>7</sup>And the king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king.<sup>8</sup>And the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, as Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. And the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" As the word left the mouth of the king, they covered Haman's face.<sup>9</sup>Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, "Moreover, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." And the king said, "Hang him on that."<sup>10</sup>So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.
7.overview: At the second feast the king asks a third time for Esther's request (vv. 1-2). She asks for her life and her people's, quoting the decree itself (vv. 3-4). Asked who has dared to do this, she points across the table: A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman! (vv. 5-6). The king goes out in fury; Haman, begging Esther for his life, is found falling on her couch (vv. 7-8). Harbona mentions the gallows built for Mordecai, and the king orders Haman hanged on it (vv. 9-10). But the decree still stands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther asks for her life and her people (vv. 1-4) and names their enemy, and Haman is terrified (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The queen who had hidden her people for five years says I and my people in one breath, and names the man at the table. The king asks who dared to do what he himself had signed.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king and Haman went in to feast with Queen Esther. And on the second day, as they were drinking wine after the feast, the king again said to Esther, "What is your wish, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you. And what is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the third time the king has asked (5:3, 6). Haman is at the table: the same Haman who this morning led Mordecai's horse through the city, went home with his head covered, and was told by his wife that he would fall. He has been hurried here with no time to think. The king is in good humour, the queen gracious. Only she knows what she is about to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Queen Esther answered, "If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be granted me for my wish, and my people for my request. For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated. If we had been sold merely as slaves, men and women, I would have been silent, for our affliction is not to be compared with the loss to the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king asked for her wish and her request, and she answers in exactly that shape: my life, and my people. She puts herself first so that the king will feel it; the threat is to his own queen. And then, my people: the secret she has kept since the day she entered the harem (2:10) is given up in two words.

To be destroyed, to be killed, and to be annihilated are the three verbs of Haman's decree, word for word (3:13). She quotes the king's own law back to him. And sold means someone paid for this (3:9). In saying I and my people she stands inside the sentence with them.

Even at the edge of death she is tactful: she would not have troubled the king over mere slavery. But this is killing. It is the moment chapter 4 fasted for, and she speaks with the courtesy of a queen and the courage of someone who has already said, if I perish, I perish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, "Who is he, and where is he, who has dared to do this?" And Esther said, "A foe and enemy! This wicked Haman!" Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer to the king's question is: you. He handed Haman the signet ring and said, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you (3:11). He never asked which people. It is a picture of how easily the powerful sign things and forget them, and how outraged they become when what they signed touches someone they love.

After five years of silence and two days of feasts, she says his name with him sitting there. The man who was filled with fury because a Jew would not tremble before him (5:9) trembles before a Jewish woman.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king storms out, and returns to find Haman fallen on the queen's couch (vv. 7-8). Harbona points to the gallows, and Haman is hanged on it (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The tree Haman raised for a righteous man held the guilty one. At the cross it was the other way round.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg for his life from Queen Esther, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king. And the king returned from the palace garden to the place where they were drinking wine, as Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was. And the king said, "Will he even assault the queen in my presence, in my own house?" As the word left the mouth of the king, they covered Haman's face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perhaps the king is furious; perhaps he is realising that the decree has his seal on it. Haman sees his death in the king's face and does the one thing left: he begs. The man who required every knee at the gate to bend is on his knees before a Jew.

Guests reclined on couches to eat. Haman, pleading, throws himself down at the queen's couch just as the king walks back in. Falling: the word Zeresh used only hours before, you will not overcome him but will surely fall before him (6:13). He falls, and it looks like the worst thing a man could do in the king's house.

That morning Haman had covered his own head in shame (6:12). Now others cover it, and it means death.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Harbona, one of the eunuchs in attendance on the king, said, "Moreover, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king, is standing at Haman's house, fifty cubits high." And the king said, "Hang him on that."
verseByVerse.commentary: We have met Harbona: he was one of the seven eunuchs sent to fetch Vashti in chapter 1 (1:10). The servant who was there when the throne was emptied is there when the enemy falls. And he adds the detail that settles it: the gallows was built for Mordecai, whose word saved the king. Last night's reading from the chronicles is known to the whole court. Haman had planned to hang the man the king was honouring, and it could not be denied, because the gallows stood in his garden for all Susa to see.

verseByVerse.quote: So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Psalms had long since described it: He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head (Ps 7:15-16). The tree Haman raised for the righteous man held Haman.

At the cross the reversal ran the opposite way. The tree that should have held the guilty held the righteous One: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal 3:13). And as with Haman's gallows, the enemy's weapon turned on the enemy: None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8). On that tree Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15).

The wrath of the king abated: the phrase used when his anger at Vashti cooled (2:1). His wrath was satisfied by the death of the guilty man. God's wrath against his people was satisfied by the death of One who was not guilty: we have now been justified by his blood, and much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God (Rom 5:9).

Yet the chapter ends with a problem unsolved. Haman is dead; his decree is not. It is still posted in every province, sealed with the king's ring, and cannot be repealed. The next chapter is about what can be done with a law that cannot be undone.

7.theology:
The enemy is undone by his own instrument, and Esther gives up her safety to stand with her people.

Haman's tree held the guilty; Christ's cross held the Righteous in the place of the guilty, and there the enemy's weapon became his defeat and God's wrath toward his people was turned away (see on vv. 9-10).
7.examples: The man who demanded that every knee bend to him ended the day begging a Jewish woman for his life. Yet the chapter closes on unfinished business: Haman died, and his decree did not.

8.title: The Edict of Reversal: Light and Joy
8.text: <sup>1</sup>On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her.<sup>2</sup>And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.<sup>3</sup>Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews.<sup>4</sup>When the king held out the golden scepter to Esther, Esther rose and stood before the king.<sup>5</sup>And she said, "If it please the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the thing seems right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the provinces of the king.<sup>6</sup>For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people? Or how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"<sup>7</sup>Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows, because he intended to lay hands on the Jews.<sup>8</sup>But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king's ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked."<sup>9</sup>The king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. And an edict was written, according to all that Mordecai commanded concerning the Jews, to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Ethiopia, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and also to the Jews in their script and their language.<sup>10</sup>And he wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring. Then he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding on swift horses that were used in the king's service, bred from the royal stud,<sup>11</sup>saying that the king allowed the Jews who were in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, children and women included, and to plunder their goods,<sup>12</sup>on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.<sup>13</sup>A copy of what was written was to be issued as a decree in every province, being publicly displayed to all peoples, and the Jews were to be ready on that day to take vengeance on their enemies.<sup>14</sup>So the couriers, mounted on their swift horses that were used in the king's service, rode out hurriedly, urged by the king's command. And the decree was issued in Susa the citadel.<sup>15</sup>Then Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal robes of blue and white, with a great golden crown and a robe of fine linen and purple, and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.<sup>16</sup>The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor.<sup>17</sup>And in every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his edict reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, a feast and a holiday. And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
8.overview: The king gives Esther Haman's house, and Mordecai, now known to be her kinsman, receives the signet ring (vv. 1-2). But the decree still stands. Esther falls at the king's feet in tears and asks that Haman's letters be revoked (vv. 3-6). The king cannot revoke a sealed edict, but lets Esther and Mordecai write another in his name (vv. 7-8). Mordecai's edict goes to every province, and to the Jews in their own script, permitting them to defend themselves against any force that attacks them on 13 Adar (vv. 9-14). Mordecai goes out in royal robes; Susa rejoices; the Jews have light and gladness and joy and honor, and many of the peoples declare themselves Jews (vv. 15-17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — An Edict Sealed with the King's Ring Cannot Be Revoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Haman's house and ring pass to Esther and Mordecai (vv. 1-2). Esther pleads in tears for her people (vv. 3-6), and the king lets them write a second edict, since a sealed one cannot be revoked (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Haman was dead and his law was alive.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her. And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same day, the house of the man who had planned to plunder every Jewish house in the empire belongs to a Jew. The sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous (Prov 13:22). And the cousin at the gate is brought into the king's presence as family.

The ring that sealed the death of the Jews is on a Jew's hand. Joseph received a ring the same way: Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand (Gen 41:42). The man who would not bow to Haman now holds Haman's authority and Haman's house.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esther spoke again to the king. She fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews. When the king held out the golden scepter to Esther, Esther rose and stood before the king. And she said, "If it please the king, and if I have found favor in his sight, and if the thing seems right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the provinces of the king. For how can I bear to see the calamity that is coming to my people? Or how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
She could have stopped. Her enemy was dead, her life safe, her cousin wearing the ring. But the decree still hung over every Jewish family in the empire, and she goes back in, not in royal robes to a feast, but at his feet in tears.

The sceptre is held out again, and she asks with every courtesy she has, and lays the blame carefully: the letters devised by Haman, not the king who sealed them.

How can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred? This is the heart of an intercessor: she is safe, and she cannot live with their danger. Paul felt the same for the same people: I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart ... for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh (Rom 9:2-3). It is worth asking whether our own safety is enough for us. The love that grieves for those not yet safe is not ours by nature; it is the love of the One who first grieved over us, poured into our hearts by his Spirit (Rom 5:5).

Christians have long seen in her a faint likeness of a greater Intercessor. Esther, safe in the palace, went back in for her people at the risk of her life. The Son of God did not stay safe in his Father's presence: he came down, laid down his life for his people, and now always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). She pleaded with a king who might refuse. He pleads with a Father who always hears him (John 11:42).

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows, because he intended to lay hands on the Jews. But you may write as you please with regard to the Jews, in the name of the king, and seal it with the king's ring, for an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the problem, stated by the king himself. He cannot cancel his own decree. The law of the Medes and Persians, which deposed Vashti, now binds the king to a massacre he no longer wants (cf. Dan 6:15). What he can do is let them write another decree, with his name and ring on it, to stand against the first.

There is a gospel shape here, and it must be drawn carefully. Haman's decree was wicked; the law's sentence on us is just. But the principle holds: a sentence that cannot be revoked must be answered, not ignored. God did not cancel the sentence on sin or pretend it was not there. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh (Rom 8:3), and then issued the word that answers it: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1).
verseByVerse.note: Compare Daniel 6:8, 12, where the same rule binds Darius.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Light and Gladness and Joy and Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new edict goes out by the swiftest couriers, letting the Jews defend their lives on the thirteenth of Adar (vv. 9-14). Mordecai goes out in royal robes, Susa rejoices, and many declare themselves Jews (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The same roads that carried mourning now carry feasts.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is the month of Sivan, on the twenty-third day. And an edict was written, according to all that Mordecai commanded concerning the Jews, to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Ethiopia, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and also to the Jews in their script and their language. And he wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring. Then he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding on swift horses that were used in the king's service, bred from the royal stud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first decree was written on the thirteenth of Nisan (3:12). Count it: seventeen days to the end of Nisan, twenty-nine of Iyyar, twenty-three of Sivan, two months and ten days. Nearly nine months remain before the thirteenth of Adar.

The same scribes, the same provinces, the same imperial post, and one addition. The first decree was sent to everyone about the Jews. This one is sent to the Jews as well, in their own letters, so that every Jewish family can read with their own eyes that they may live. It goes on the best horses in the empire: the news of life travels faster than the news of death did.

verseByVerse.quote: saying that the king allowed the Jews who were in every city to gather and defend their lives, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, children and women included, and to plunder their goods, on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put this beside 3:13 and you will see that Mordecai has turned Haman's decree round, verb for verb: to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate. The first decree licensed anyone to kill Jews. This one licenses Jews to defend themselves against anyone who tries.

Did the decree allow killing women and children? The phrase children and women included is hard, and readers should know it is disputed. The ESV rendering suggests so: it may mirror Haman's decree (3:13) and mean the families of the attackers. Or it may belong with the word them, meaning the Jews' own children and women whom the armed force would attack. Either way, the decree is for defence: it is aimed at any armed force ... that might attack them. And when the day comes, chapter 9 speaks of men killed in Susa (9:6, 15) and of those who hated them in the provinces (9:16), and three times says the Jews laid no hand on the plunder they had been permitted (9:10, 15, 16). The likeliest reading is that the right granted was self-defence, and that they used it with restraint.

verseByVerse.quote: A copy of what was written was to be issued as a decree in every province, being publicly displayed to all peoples, and the Jews were to be ready on that day to take vengeance on their enemies. So the couriers, mounted on their swift horses that were used in the king's service, rode out hurriedly, urged by the king's command. And the decree was issued in Susa the citadel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beside the old notice in every town square goes up a new one, sent in the same hurry as before (3:15). Anyone who read the first and sharpened a knife would now read the second.

“Take vengeance” here means lawful retribution on a decreed day against those who attacked, not private revenge. The Hebrew word is used of a ruler's justice as well as of personal revenge, and the decree gives no licence beyond the day and beyond those who came to kill.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal robes of blue and white, with a great golden crown and a robe of fine linen and purple, and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blue and white, fine linen and purple: the colours of the palace hangings in chapter 1 (1:6). The man who sat at the gate in sackcloth and ashes (4:1) walks out dressed like the palace itself. Last time he wore royal robes it was for a morning, with Haman leading his horse (6:11). These are his own.

When Haman's decree went out, the city of Susa was thrown into confusion (3:15). Now it shouted and rejoiced. When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices (Prov 11:10).

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews had light and gladness and joy and honor. And in every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his edict reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, a feast and a holiday. And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Count the words. When the first decree arrived, the Jews had four: mourning ... fasting and weeping and lamenting (4:3). Now they have four others: light and gladness and joy and honor. Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart (Ps 97:11). Anyone who has lived under a sentence (a diagnosis, a debt, a guilt that would not go away) and then heard it answered knows what the Jews of Susa felt that day.

Wherever the king's command and his edict reached is the phrase of 4:3: the couriers who had carried mourning along those roads now carried feasts.

The book is honest about the motive: fear of the Jews. Some no doubt only wanted to be on the winning side. But the prophets had seen a day when the nations would join this people: ten men from the nations of every tongue shall take hold of the robe of a Jew, saying, Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you (Zech 8:23). The Christian reader sees where that ends: a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb (Rev 7:9).

8.theology:
A decree that cannot be revoked must be answered by a decree of equal authority. God has done with the just sentence on sinners what the Persian king could not do with an unjust one: carried it out on his own Son and issued the answering word of no condemnation (see on vv. 7-8).

Esther will not rest in her own safety while her kindred are in danger. Mourning is turned to light and joy, and the nations begin to attach themselves to God's people, as the prophets foresaw.
8.examples: The reversals come one after another: Haman's house belonged to a Jew that same day, and the ring that had sealed the death of the Jews was on Mordecai's hand. Esther, safe herself, went back in, in tears, for her people.

9.title: The Great Reversal: Victory and the Feast of Purim
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.<sup>2</sup>The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. And no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples.<sup>3</sup>All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the royal agents also helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.<sup>4</sup>For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces, for the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.<sup>5</sup>The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.<sup>6</sup>In Susa the citadel itself the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men,<sup>7</sup>and also killed Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha<sup>8</sup>and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha<sup>9</sup>and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha,<sup>10</sup>the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they laid no hand on the plunder.<sup>11</sup>That very day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king.<sup>12</sup>And the king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and also the ten sons of Haman. What then have they done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what further is your request? It shall be fulfilled."<sup>13</sup>And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to do according to this day's edict. And let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows."<sup>14</sup>So the king commanded this to be done. 9.overview: On 13 Adar, the day Haman's lot had chosen, the reverse occurred: the Jews gather in every province to defend themselves, and the officials help them for fear of Mordecai (vv. 1-4). In Susa they kill 500 men and the ten sons of Haman (vv. 5-10). Esther asks for a second day in Susa and the public hanging of Haman's sons; 300 more are killed in Susa and 75,000 enemies in the provinces, but no plunder is taken (vv. 11-16). They rest and feast on the fourteenth, in Susa on the fifteenth (vv. 17-19). Mordecai makes both days an annual feast, with gifts of food and gifts to the poor, named Purim after Haman's Pur; Esther confirms it in writing (vv. 20-32).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the thirteenth of Adar the reverse occurred (v. 1). The Jews gather in every city, helped by the officials (vv. 2-4), and in Susa they strike down their enemies and Haman's sons (vv. 5-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The day chosen by lot for the Jews' destruction became the day of their deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's command and edict were about to be carried out, on the very day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to gain the mastery over them, the reverse occurred: the Jews gained mastery over those who hated them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleven months since the lot was cast, this is the day Haman's dice chose. And the book gives its whole theology in one phrase: the reverse occurred, literally, it was overturned. The narrator does not say who reversed it, because every reader who has come this far knows.

That is still how God works for his people. The cross was the day the enemies of God thought they had won. None of the rulers of this age understood this (1 Cor 2:8). On that day too, the reverse occurred.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who sought their harm. And no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples. All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the royal agents also helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them. For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread throughout all the provinces, for the man Mordecai grew more and more powerful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They gathered, as the second decree allowed. The fear of them had fallen is what Rahab said to the spies at Jericho: the fear of you has fallen upon us (Josh 2:9). Something about this people, when God was with them, made their enemies lose heart.

The same officials who had posted Haman's decree now protected its intended victims. The man who a year before had sat at the gate in sackcloth was the most feared man in the empire's administration.

Grew more and more powerful echoes David's rise: And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him (2 Sam 5:10). The narrator borrows the sentence and stops before its last clause. He expects the reader who knows it to finish it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them, and did as they pleased to those who hated them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the hard verse of the book, and it should not be hurried past. Look first at who is struck: their enemies, those who hated them, those who sought their harm (v. 2). Haman's decree was still law. In every province there were men who had waited eleven months for the day they could kill Jewish families and take their houses, and on that day they came. The Jews met them. Did as they pleased is the book's recurring phrase (1:8), and here it means that for once the power was not in the hands of those who hated them.

Was this right? A plain reader will ask, and should. Three things can be said honestly. First, this was not a massacre of the innocent turned round. Haman's law, never cancelled, let anyone kill every Jew, children included (3:13), and on that day men came to use it. The Jews were allowed to meet any armed force ... that might attack them (8:11), and the dead are named as those who hated them. To defend one's family from men coming to kill them is not murder (Exodus 22:2 assumes a householder may defend his house). Second, the narrator reports without cheering: there is no victory song over the slain. Third, Scripture records Esther and Mordecai truly without asking us to approve every request, and the second day in Susa (v. 13) remains hard. What the book wants us to see is that God did not let his people be wiped out, for the promise of a Saviour ran through them. None of it is a pattern for the church, which is given no sword to wield for Christ (Romans 12:19).

verseByVerse.quote: In Susa the citadel itself the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men, and also killed Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha, the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, but they laid no hand on the plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Hebrew scrolls these ten names are written in a column by themselves, one under another. Haman had boasted to his friends of the number of his sons (5:11). Here they are, counted.

The second decree had allowed them plunder (8:11), and they did not touch it; the book says so three times (vv. 10, 15, 16). Why the insistence? Saul, sent against Amalek, spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen (1 Sam 15:9), and Samuel asked him, Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD? (1 Sam 15:19). Saul lost his kingdom over the plunder of Amalek. Now a Benjaminite of the line of Kish (2:5) faces the Agagite's house again, and this time no one takes a thing. This was not greed dressed up as self-defence. They fought for their lives and went home with nothing else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — They Laid No Hands on the Plunder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Esther asks for one more day in Susa and for the bodies of Haman's sons to be hanged (vv. 11-14). In Susa and the provinces the Jews defend their lives against those who hated them (vv. 15-16), then rest and feast (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The sons of Kish, facing the house of Agag, refused exactly what Saul had taken.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day the number of those killed in Susa the citadel was reported to the king. And the king said to Queen Esther, "In Susa the citadel the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and also the ten sons of Haman. What then have they done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your wish? It shall be granted you. And what further is your request? It shall be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the fourth time the king asks her (5:3; 5:6; 7:2). The king who once gave away a people without asking their name now reckons up the dead of his own capital and asks the Jewish queen what more she wants.

verseByVerse.quote: And Esther said, "If it please the king, let the Jews who are in Susa be allowed tomorrow also to do according to this day's edict. And let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows." So the king commanded this to be done. A decree was issued in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This request troubles many readers, and honestly so. We are not told why Esther asked. What the text shows is that there were still enemies in Susa: the next day the Jews killed three hundred more (v. 15). And the sons were already dead (v. 10); hanging their bodies was the ancient way of making a public end of a house, so that no one could doubt that Haman's line was finished. The narrator neither praises the request nor condemns it. Esther is not presented as sinless anywhere in this book, and we are not asked to make her so.

The chapter describes a persecuted minority, under a king's decree, defending itself on the day its enemies had been told they could kill it; as said above, it is no pattern for the church.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews who were in Susa gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and they killed 300 men in Susa, but they laid no hands on the plunder. Now the rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives, and got relief from their enemies and killed 75,000 of those who hated them, but they laid no hands on the plunder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seventy-five thousand across 127 provinces is a terrible number, and the text does not make it pleasant. (The Greek Old Testament gives 15,000; the Hebrew, which our Bibles follow, has 75,000. Either figure, spread across an empire, describes many local attacks beaten off, not one battle.) But see how it is framed: to defend their lives, against those who hated them, and with no hand laid on the plunder.

And they got relief, and then rested (v. 17). Moses had joined rest from enemies, the end of Amalek and a memory never to be lost (Deut 25:19), and all three are in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth day they rested and made that a day of feasting and gladness. But the Jews who were in Susa gathered on the thirteenth day and on the fourteenth, and rested on the fifteenth day, making that a day of feasting and gladness. Therefore the Jews of the villages, who live in the rural towns, hold the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day for gladness and feasting, as a holiday, and as a day on which they send gifts of food to one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews of Susa, who fought two days, rested on the fifteenth: hence Purim's two dates, and the later custom of a second day in walled cities.

The feast is not the day of the fighting but the day after, the day they rested. Purim does not celebrate killing. It celebrates rest: the morning a people woke up and found they were still alive.

Sending portions to one another is the custom Nehemiah commanded at the reading of the law (Neh 8:10, 12): joy is meant to be shared.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–32 — These Days Should Be Remembered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mordecai makes the two days a yearly feast (vv. 20-23), named Purim after Haman's lot (vv. 24-26), to be kept in every generation (vv. 27-28), and Esther confirms it in writing (vv. 29-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Amalek's memory ended, and the memory of deliverance was written down to last.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far, obliging them to keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar and also the fifteenth day of the same, year by year, as the days on which the Jews got relief from their enemies, and as the month that had been turned for them from sorrow into gladness and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, days for sending gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Letters go down the same roads again, this time about a feast. Turned says again what verse 1 said: the reverse occurred. The psalm says it of one man: You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness (Ps 30:11). Mordecai had worn the sackcloth (4:1) and then the royal robes (8:15). And Jesus promised it to his disciples the night before the cross: You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy (John 16:20).

The deliverance was to be remembered with generosity: gifts to the poor. Nobody was to be left out of the feast because they could not afford it. Those who have been given so much give.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews accepted what they had started to do, and what Mordecai had written to them. For Haman the Agagite, the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur (that is, cast lots), to crush and to destroy them. But when it came before the king, he gave orders in writing that his evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They had already begun to feast; Mordecai made it law. Then the whole book in two sentences: Haman's evil plan ... should return on his own head. And again the psalm: His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends (Ps 7:16).

When it came before the king can equally be read, in Hebrew, “when she came” before the king. Either way, the turning point was the queen who went in uncalled, if I perish, I perish (4:16), and the plot that died when it was brought into the king's presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they called these days Purim, after the term Pur. Therefore, because of all that was written in this letter, and of what they had faced in this matter, and of what had happened to them, the Jews firmly obligated themselves and their offspring and all who joined them, that without fail they would keep these two days according to what was written and at the time appointed every year, that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, in every clan, province, and city, and that these days of Purim should never fall into disuse among the Jews, nor should the commemoration of these days cease among their descendants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Purim means Haman's lots. The very device he used to choose the day of their death gave its name to the feast of their deliverance. His dice are remembered every year, and only as the joke that God made of them.

And all who joined them: the people who had declared themselves Jews (8:17) are included in the feast.

God had once told Moses to write this as a memorial in a book that he would blot out the memory of Amalek (Exod 17:14). Here Amalek's memory ends and Israel's memory begins.

The church has a feast of remembrance too, instituted on the night before the greatest reversal of all: Do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19). As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Cor 11:26). God's people keep remembering who turned their sorrow into joy.

Should Christians keep Purim? It was a Jewish festival not commanded in the law of Moses. Christians are free to remember it, but no day binds the conscience (Rom 14:5; Col 2:16–17). Its message belongs to us: God keeps his people, unseen, through ordinary events.
verseByVerse.note: Purim is still celebrated by Jews each year, with the reading of Esther.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Queen Esther, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew gave full written authority, confirming this second letter about Purim. Letters were sent to all the Jews, to the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, in words of peace and truth, that these days of Purim should be observed at their appointed seasons, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther obligated them, and as they had obligated themselves and their offspring, with regard to their fasts and their lamenting. The command of Esther confirmed these practices of Purim, and it was recorded in writing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her father's name for the second time in the book (2:15). The orphan girl who hid her people now writes to all of them, in her own name, with the authority of a queen.

In words of peace and truth, with fasts and lamenting turned into feasts: all of it is in Zechariah's promise that the fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth ... shall be to the house of Judah seasons of joy and gladness and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace (Zech 8:19). And the fasts are not forgotten. The feast remembers the sackcloth that came before it.

It is written in a book, like Mordecai's deed (2:23) that was read on the sleepless night (6:1). This book has been about what gets written down and who remembers it. God's name was never written in it. His faithfulness is on every page.

9.theology:
The day chosen for destruction is overturned into the day of deliverance, and the enemy's own lot names the feast. The Jews defend their lives and refuse the plunder Saul once took; the feast is kept on the day of rest, not of battle.

Sorrow turned into joy is the shape of the gospel, and the church keeps its own feast of remembrance. But the church does not take up the sword for Christ: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4). In Esther the old enmity between Agag and Israel ends with the sword. In Christ God ends hostility another way, reconciling enemies to himself and to one another through the cross, thereby killing the hostility (Ephesians 2:16), so that the feast of the gospel is kept by Jew and Gentile together.
9.examples: Purim is kept on the day they rested, not the day they fought, with gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor, so that no one is left out of the joy.

10.title: Mordecai's Greatness and the Hidden Hand Revealed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>King Ahasuerus imposed tax on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.<sup>2</sup>And all the acts of his power and might, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?<sup>3</sup>For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.
10.overview: The book closes briefly. Ahasuerus taxes his empire (v. 1); his deeds and Mordecai's honour are recorded in the chronicles of Media and Persia (v. 2); and Mordecai, second only to the king, is loved by his people, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people (v. 3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — He Sought the Welfare of His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Taxes, chronicles and a man second only to the king: the book ends quietly (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: The book that opened on a king displaying his glory closes on a Jew using his power for the good of others. God is not named in the last sentence either. Peace is.

verseByVerse.quote: King Ahasuerus imposed tax on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary: It is an odd way to end, and a true one. The empire goes on; the taxes are collected; the Jews are still subjects of a Persian king. The deliverance was real, and it was not the kingdom of God. God's people still live in someone else's empire, as in every age until the King comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the acts of his power and might, and the full account of the high honor of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is how the books of Kings close each reign: are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (1 Kgs 14:29). Esther ends like a king's story, and the name beside the emperor's is a Jew's. It is the same book where Mordecai's unrewarded deed was filed (2:23) and read aloud on the sleepless night (6:1). The man who got a line in the annals now has a full account.

The chronicles are lost, though Persian tablets name officials called Marduka.

verseByVerse.quote: For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mordecai is second in the empire, as Joseph had been in Egypt: only as regards the throne will I be greater than you (Gen 41:40). And the last words are not about his rank but what he did with it. Haman used power to destroy a people; Mordecai used it to seek their good.

Sought the welfare is the language of Jeremiah's letter to the first exiles: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jer 29:7). The book, true to itself to the last line, gives us Jeremiah's words without the prayer and without the Name. The reader who has come this far can supply both.

A greater King has one at his right hand who is not second to him but one with him (Heb 1:3), and of whom Zechariah said, he shall speak peace to the nations (Zech 9:10). He came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near (Eph 2:17). Mordecai spoke peace to his own people. Christ speaks it to everyone who comes to him, and his reign has no end.

Catholic and Orthodox Bibles continue the book after this verse with Mordecai's dream. These are additions made in the Greek translation; the Hebrew book ends here, as Protestant Bibles do.

10.theology: True greatness is power used for the good of others. Mordecai spoke peace to his people; the King whom Zechariah promised speaks peace to the nations.
10.examples: The last chapter opens with taxes, and the last word of the book is peace.
